# PPJ language reference

PPJ is OfficeKit's single public presentation authoring language. It is one
UTF-8 strict JSON file with schema `office-kit/ppj/v1`. Edit the file, then
use the CLI to validate, build, render and review it. JavaScript may generate
JSON externally, but JavaScript functions, JSON5, raw OOXML, XPath, relationship
IDs, network calls and executable expressions are not PPJ.

## Workflows

```text
new deck:       deck.ppj → check → build → render → review
third-party:    input.pptx → import → inspect/edit deck.ppj → build
OfficeKit PPTX: authored.pptx → import → exact embedded PPJ recovery
durable task:   add --task only when immutable revision/resume evidence is wanted
```

The CLI is `officekit ppj import|inspect|check|build|render|review`. Build
never overwrites the PPJ or its bound source. Render and review are explicit;
successful compilation is not visual approval.

## Root fields

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema` | yes | Fixed language identifier `office-kit/ppj/v1`. |
| `meta` | yes | Stable program identity, title, language and revision version. |
| `intent` | yes | Audience, brief, narrative, editorial constraints and delivery purpose. |
| `design` | yes | Canvas, theme, named styles, deck-specific Design Grammar and motion policy. |
| `assets` | no | Content-addressed local resources with rights and accessibility metadata. |
| `source` | no | Optional immutable third-party PPTX binding for source-preserving edits. |
| `components` | no | Finite reusable structures with parameters, slots, variants, repeat and simple conditions. |
| `pages` | yes | Ordered slides; each page's element array is the real back-to-front z-order. |
| `sections` | no | Persistent section membership over stable page IDs. |
| `customShows` | no | Named ordered page subsets. |
| `comments` | no | Persistent presentation comments supported by the language contract. |

All objects are closed: undeclared fields fail validation. IDs match
`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]*$` and remain stable across edits. Coordinates and
sizes use points. Page order is `pages[]` order. Element order is back-to-front
`pages[].elements[]` order; do not invent a second z-index.

Simple text uses a string. Mixed formatting uses `paragraphs[]` and
`runs[]`; do not encode markup inside strings. Colors use theme references or
explicit typed color objects. Assets use relative URIs, exact MIME and SHA-256;
remote URLs and data-fetch instructions are invalid. Accessibility and rights
metadata travel with the asset or element.

### Native inline formulas

Use a formula run only when mathematical structure is part of the evidence.
Keep surrounding prose as ordinary text runs and omit `\(` / `\)`
delimiters:

```json
{
  "runs": [
    { "text": "Expected loss: " },
    {
      "id": "loss-equation",
      "formula": {
        "syntax": "latex",
        "source": "\\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \\cdot L_i"
      },
      "style": { "size": 24, "color": "#172033" }
    }
  ]
}
```

This is a finite formula language, not TeX execution. It supports literals,
groups, subscript and superscript, `\frac`, square-root `\sqrt`, common
Greek letters and symbols, `\int` / `\sum` / `\prod`, roman text via
`\mathrm` / `\text` / `\operatorname`, common functions, bounded
spacing, and ordinary `\left` / `\right` delimiters. The source budget is
4,096 characters, 512 tokens, 32 nesting levels and 2,048 AST nodes.

Macros, environments, packages, conditionals, counters, I/O, matrices,
alignment, color commands and unknown commands fail before PPTX output. A
formula run may declare only `size` and solid `color`; it cannot carry a
hyperlink, font override, highlight, gradient, shadow or text decoration. The
compiler writes editable native `a14:m` / OMML, not SVG, PNG, a formula font
or literal backslash text.

Exact LaTeX recovery depends on the embedded PPJ snapshot. Importing an
ordinary third-party formula does not authorize OfficeKit to infer LaTeX from
OMML; the native graph remains preserved and unsupported edits fail closed.

### Element visibility and edit locks

Every typed element may declare `hidden` and `locked`. `hidden: true` keeps
the element and stable ID in PPJ but hides that object in the slide; it does not
hide the page or move the object in z-order. `locked: true` applies OfficeKit's
canonical edit lock for that object kind. It helps protect a finished visual
layer from accidental selection or movement, but it is not document security,
encryption, or an access-control boundary. Element array order remains the only
z-order.

Imported objects may change these fields only when their `nativeRef` issues
`setHidden` or `setLocked` for the current source revision. A partial or
extension-bearing native lock profile remains source-owned and does not become
an editable boolean.

## Preset geometry adjustments

complete ordered integer array. Omit it or use `[]` for the native preset
defaults. Percentage-like values use 100000 as 100%; angle values use 60000
units per degree. PPJ derives native guide names from the preset and never
exposes formula strings. The catalog contains 178
PPJ names; availability does not make a shape useful, so choose geometry by

## Authored compiler availability

Schema validity proves that a program belongs to the PPJ language; it does not
claim that every declared state already has a source-free native writer. The
compiler owns ordinary text, shapes with preset geometry and solid fills,
images and native image backgrounds, charts, tables, connectors, groups,
placeholders, notes, comments, sections, custom shows, transitions, animations
and Morph subject to the explicit boundaries below. A boundary fails before
writing output; imported native content remains source-preserved.

## Components terminate

Components have a finite frame, typed parameters, named slots, explicit
variants, bounded repeat items and only `equals`, `notEquals`, `present`
or `absent` conditions. They cannot call themselves recursively. Expanded
IDs are deterministic. A component is reuse, not a hidden script.

## Imported PPTX and nativeRef

Import copies the source package into a content-addressed local asset and binds
its SHA-256. Every visible object becomes a typed element or `opaque` with a
`nativeRef`. A nativeRef lists only capability-issued fields. Edit those
fields and keep its expected revision/hash; unsupported topology stays opaque.
No-op build returns the source bytes exactly. A stale, ambiguous or undeclared
mutation fails instead of rebuilding or flattening the source.

### Imported presentation canvas

An imported `design.canvas` is editable only when its own `nativeRef` issues
`setCanvas` for `canvas.width` and `canvas.height`. Values stay in points.
Keep the nativeRef unchanged, edit one or both dimensions, then build and
re-import. The compiler changes only the native presentation canvas: it never
scales, reflows, crops or moves slide, layout, master or element coordinates.
Because every page is composed against that canvas, render and review every
page for exposed margins, clipping and changed balance after the edit.

### Imported raster/SVG fallback pairs

PowerPoint may store one visible picture as a raster compatibility fallback
plus an SVG used by modern hosts. PPJ projects these as two local assets:

- `image.asset` is the raster fallback;
- `image.svgAsset` is the true SVG member.

Change `svgAsset` only when that image's `nativeRef` issues `replaceSvg` for
`image.svgAsset`. Declare the replacement as a new content-addressed local
`image/svg+xml` asset, keep `asset`, the image ID and nativeRef unchanged,
then build and re-import. PPJ cannot add or remove the pair and does not invent
a raster fallback. Review the modern SVG render; when an older host matters,
record separately that its unchanged raster fallback may still show the prior
artwork.

An imported native leaf has a stable opaque ID, a closed kind, the expected
source-value hash and its current scalar value. Change only `value`; never
invent an ID, kind or hash:

```json
{
  "nativeRef": {
    "handle": "nr-…",
    "sourceSha256": "<64 lowercase hex>",
    "revision": "pptx-…",
    "objectHash": "<64 lowercase hex>",
    "capabilitySetSha256": "<64 lowercase hex>",
    "capabilities": [],
    "leaves": [
      {
        "id": "leaf-font-size-…",
        "kind": "fontSizePoints",
        "expectedHash": "<64 lowercase hex>",
        "value": 18
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

For an imported deck, change `pages[]` order only when every moved page's
`nativeRef` advertises `reorder` with `pageOrder`. The projected page ID is
anchored to its source SlidePart, and unchanged page-local element IDs survive
the move. This is distinct from element `reorder/zOrder`, which changes the
stack inside one page. Do not combine page deletion and reorder in one build.
If modeled `sections[]` exist, update their `pages` arrays in the same program
so they still form one complete partition in the new presentation order.
Comments and custom shows keep referring to the same stable page IDs. An
opaque section graph receives no page-order capability and remains unchanged.

To reuse one complete imported page, find a page whose `nativeRef` advertises
`duplicate` with `pageClone`. Insert one fresh page immediately after that
source page with an empty `elements` array and
`sourceClone: { page: "<source-page-id>", capability: "<issued-capability-id>" }`.
Do not copy nativeRef, element state, layout, background, notes, transition,
animation or visibility into the pending clone. Build and re-import first; the
new SlidePart then projects as an ordinary source-bound page whose full typed
or opaque content can be inspected and edited through its newly issued
capabilities. One source page may have only one pending clone, and the same
build cannot also delete/reorder pages or change section/custom-show routes.

To reuse one exact top-level component instead of the full page, add
`retainElement: "<source-element-id>"` to that same `sourceClone`. The ID
must name one direct entry in the source page's `elements[]`; keep the owning
top-level group when the desired object is nested. Every omitted sibling must
freshly advertise `delete` with `element`. The compiler retains the selected
native graph unchanged and lowers all sibling removals through the existing
deletion proofs. The pending page stays empty until build and re-import, when
the retained component becomes an ordinary source-bound typed or opaque node
with fresh nativeRef capabilities. This is not arbitrary graph extraction and
does not port the JavaScript repeated-candidate workflow into PPJ.

To continue an ordinary imported page without cloning it, require the page's
`nativeRef` to advertise `appendElement` with `elements`. Keep every
source-projected element unchanged and in its original order, then append new
typed elements at the end of `pages[].elements[]`. This suffix is above all
source-owned objects. The bounded profile accepts `text`, `image`, and
`shape` only when the shape preset is `rect`, `roundRect`, or `ellipse`;
the text type lowers to the native textbox profile. New elements have fresh
IDs and no nativeRef. Do not interleave them with native elements, add a paired
SVG fallback, or combine the append with another source mutation. Build and
re-import before the next edit so the new native objects receive fresh stable
source-bound IDs and capability evidence.

For imported object motion, change the complete `pages[].animations[]` array
only when that page's `nativeRef` advertises `setAnimations` with
`animations`. The capability is issued only for an absent safely addable
timing graph or an existing canonical editable graph, and never for a Morph
page. Targets remain stable PPJ element IDs; the compiler privately resolves
their current native bindings, including supported group descendants. Opaque
third-party timing receives no capability and remains byte-preserved. Build
and re-import a newly appended overlay before using it as an animation target.
Structural round-trip is not desktop playback evidence.

OfficeKit-authored PPTX embeds canonical PPJ and a node map. Import restores
that PPJ exactly when valid. If native software changed the PPTX but left the
embedded program, PPJ remains authoritative; a future build writes a new output
and never overwrites the input.

## Hard budgets

| Budget | Limit |
| --- | ---: |
| PPJ UTF-8 bytes | 16777216 |
| pages | 512 |
| expanded elements | 100000 |
| one repeat | 1024 |
| component expansion depth | 16 |

Budget, reference, type, cycle and source-capability errors are reported before
compilation. `ppj check --fix` may normalize deterministic formatting; it
must not choose layout, rewrite copy or change design semantics.

Import copies the source package into a content-addressed local asset and binds
its SHA-256. Every visible object becomes a typed element or `opaque` with a
`nativeRef`. A nativeRef lists only capability-issued fields. Edit those
fields and keep its expected revision/hash; unsupported topology stays opaque.
No-op build returns the source bytes exactly. A stale, ambiguous or undeclared
mutation fails instead of rebuilding or flattening the source.

### Imported presentation canvas

An imported `design.canvas` is editable only when its own `nativeRef` issues
`setCanvas` for `canvas.width` and `canvas.height`. Values stay in points.
Keep the nativeRef unchanged, edit one or both dimensions, then build and
re-import. The compiler changes only the native presentation canvas: it never
scales, reflows, crops or moves slide, layout, master or element coordinates.
Because every page is composed against that canvas, render and review every
page for exposed margins, clipping and changed balance after the edit.

### Imported raster/SVG fallback pairs

PowerPoint may store one visible picture as a raster compatibility fallback
plus an SVG used by modern hosts. PPJ projects these as two local assets:

- `image.asset` is the raster fallback;
- `image.svgAsset` is the true SVG member.

Change `svgAsset` only when that image's `nativeRef` issues `replaceSvg` for
`image.svgAsset`. Declare the replacement as a new content-addressed local
`image/svg+xml` asset, keep `asset`, the image ID and nativeRef unchanged,
then build and re-import. PPJ cannot add or remove the pair and does not invent
a raster fallback. Review the modern SVG render; when an older host matters,
record separately that its unchanged raster fallback may still show the prior
artwork.

top-level group when the desired object is nested. Every omitted sibling must
freshly advertise `delete` with `element`. The compiler retains the selected
native graph unchanged and lowers all sibling removals through the existing
deletion proofs. The pending page stays empty until build and re-import, when
the retained component becomes an ordinary source-bound typed or opaque node
with fresh nativeRef capabilities. This is not arbitrary graph extraction and
does not port the JavaScript repeated-candidate workflow into PPJ.

To continue an ordinary imported page without cloning it, require the page's
`nativeRef` to advertise `appendElement` with `elements`. Keep every
source-projected element unchanged and in its original order, then append new
typed elements at the end of `pages[].elements[]`. This suffix is above all
source-owned objects. The bounded profile accepts `text`, `image`, and
`shape` only when the shape preset is `rect`, `roundRect`, or `ellipse`;
the text type lowers to the native textbox profile. New elements have fresh
IDs and no nativeRef. Do not interleave them with native elements, add a paired
SVG fallback, or combine the append with another source mutation. Build and
re-import before the next edit so the new native objects receive fresh stable
source-bound IDs and capability evidence.

For imported object motion, change the complete `pages[].animations[]` array
only when that page's `nativeRef` advertises `setAnimations` with
`animations`. The capability is issued only for an absent safely addable
timing graph or an existing canonical editable graph, and never for a Morph
page. Targets remain stable PPJ element IDs; the compiler privately resolves
their current native bindings, including supported group descendants. Opaque
third-party timing receives no capability and remains byte-preserved. Build
and re-import a newly appended overlay before using it as an animation target.
Structural round-trip is not desktop playback evidence.

OfficeKit-authored PPTX embeds canonical PPJ and a node map. Import restores
that PPJ exactly when valid. If native software changed the PPTX but left the
embedded program, PPJ remains authoritative; a future build writes a new output
and never overwrites the input.

--- CHARTS REF 1 ---
# Charts and tables

Choose the visual from the relationship the audience must understand.

| Relationship | Prefer |
| --- | --- |
| trend or change over ordered time | line, area, or ordered columns |
| changing composition and total magnitude over ordered time | streamgraph |
| magnitude across categories | bars or columns with a common baseline |
| small exact counts where one repeated glyph has a declared unit | pictographic bar or column |
| distribution or correlation | scatter, bubble, or distribution view |
| intensity across two categorical dimensions | heatmap |
| open/high/low/close movement over ordered periods | candlestick |
| hierarchical part-to-whole allocation | treemap |
| hierarchical part-to-whole path across concentric levels | sunburst |
| conserved magnitude moving through a directed process | sankey |
| multivariate profile across a small shared scale | standard radar |
| contribution to change | waterfall |
| precise lookup or rule comparison | table |
| mixed measures sharing a truthful category axis | deliberate combo chart |

Avoid pies with many categories, decorative 3D, dual axes without a necessary
and clearly labelled relationship, truncated scales that exaggerate change,
and a chart that merely repeats one large number.

## Evidence integrity

- Preserve source values, units, time windows, denominators, and uncertainty.
- Use direct labels where they reduce legend lookup.
- Keep common scales for comparisons that claim comparability.
- Show missing values and estimates honestly.
- Put the exact source and as-of date on the page or in a visible source area.

Treat native data-label defaults as unsafe. Configure `showValue`,
`showCategory`, `showSeries`, and `showPercent` explicitly at the smallest
scope that communicates the claim. Keep a series name in one legend or
heading, not repeated beside every mark. For endpoint-only evidence, use two
endpoint marks or a visibly two-point comparison; never let a renderer bridge
missing categories into an invented continuous trend. Render the chart at
final size and remove any label collision before delivery, even when structural
review passes.

When a series contains only two observations, prefer a separate endpoint
comparison instead of adding a sparse line to a multi-series time axis. The
comparison may be two large values, a dumbbell without intermediate ticks, or a
two-category bar chart (`baseline`, `current`). State the exact observation
window in the heading and keep the unrelated chart's scale independent. A
shared-axis sparse line requires an explicit user request and a render proving
that the host preserves a gap; a valid PPJ shape is not evidence of a truthful
trend.

Use JSON `null` for a genuinely missing Y observation. OfficeKit keeps the
logical point count and writes a native chart gap; it does not coerce the value
to zero or invent an estimate. This works for the bounded authored chart
families, including numeric scatter/bubble Y values. Numeric `xValues` and
`bubbleSizes` remain complete arrays. In a source-bound chart, edit measured
values around an existing gap, but do not add or remove gaps: missing-point
topology remains tied to the exact source cache.

Lines, markers, labels, confidence intervals, error bars, and decision
thresholds are protected foreground evidence. Bars, areas, fills, masks, and
annotations may not hide them. For truthful combo charts, first keep the real
shared plot, render the line above pale or transparent bars, reserve clearance
around markers, and re-anchor only colliding labels. Split into aligned panels
only when the units are incompatible or the truthful shared plot remains
illegible after those repairs.

Do not force separation merely to make a checker quiet. Do not change scale,
data, or category position to manufacture whitespace.

## PPJ structure

Chart elements keep a stable `id`, explicit `frame`, typed `chartType`, data,
and style. Tables declare column widths and typed rows; they are not collections
of manually aligned text boxes. Use chart/table styles to define semantic
roles, then override only when a specific datum needs emphasis.

Chart and table frames may use `rotation`, `flipH`, and `flipV`. These are real
native graphic-frame transforms and survive PPJ build, import, and a
capability-issued source edit. Prefer ordinary zero-degree evidence layouts;
rotate a chart or table only when the orientation itself communicates a real
spatial relationship, never to decorate a page.

The authored chart compiler owns these native visual controls:

- bar, column, line, area, pie, doughnut, scatter, bubble, standard radar,
  bounded semantic waterfall, bounded vector heatmap, bounded vector
  candlestick, bounded vector streamgraph, bounded vector pictographic bars and
  columns, bounded vector treemap, bounded vector sunburst, bounded vector
  sankey, bounded column-line-area category combo plots, and bounded editable
  scatter/bubble plus line/area/column numeric overlays;
- legend visibility and top, bottom, left, or right placement;
- ordinary, stacked, and percent-stacked grouping where the chart family
  supports it;
- pie/doughnut first-slice orientation from 0 through 360 degrees and
  doughnut center-hole size from 10 through 90 percent;
- bubble scale from 0 through 300 percent and native size interpretation by
  bubble area or width;
- bar direction, gap width, category/value-axis visibility, major gridlines,
  data-label visibility and bounded label position;
- presence-aware axis reversal plus direct RGB/no-fill axis and major-grid
  lines with bounded width, dash, opacity, cap, and join;
- chart-area, plot-area, and series none, solid, or bounded direct-RGB gradient
  fills, including solid and per-stop opacity;
- editable series line width, dash, opacity, cap, join, and bounded markers;
- category/value-axis titles, number formats, label interval, tick-label
  typeface, size, bold, italic and direct RGB/alpha, value bounds and major
  unit; bounded combo charts may declare the matching secondary pair;
- chart-title Latin/East Asian typeface, size, bold, italic and direct
  RGB/alpha plus canonical line-chart smoothing and direct color variation;
- structured data labels for value, category, series, percentage, native
  position, direct number format and bounded typography at plot, series and
  sparse point scope;
- sparse point fill, outline and pie/doughnut explosion for measured exceptions;
- direct marker symbol, size, RGB/alpha fill and bounded stroke;
- exponential, linear, logarithmic, moving-average, polynomial and power
  trendlines on bar, column and line series;
- fixed-value, percentage, standard-deviation and standard-error error bars on
  bar, column and line series.

Use the analytical fields as chart semantics, not as decorative paint. A
typical evidence series can be expressed without replacing the chart with
shapes:

```json
{
  "xAxis": {
    "title": "Quarter",
    "tickLabelInterval": 1,
    "axisLine": { "color": "#16697A", "width": 1 }
  },
  "yAxis": {
    "title": "Conversion rate",
    "numberFormat": "0.0%",
    "min": 0,
    "max": 0.4,
    "majorUnit": 0.1,
    "gridLine": { "color": "#D8E1E8", "width": 0.75, "dash": "dot" }
  },
  "style": {
    "dataLabels": {
      "showValue": true,
      "position": "outside-end",
      "numberFormat": "0.0%"
    }
  },
  "data": {
    "categories": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
    "series": [{
      "id": "conversion",
      "name": "Conversion",
      "values": [0.18, 0.22, 0.27, 0.31],
      "marker": { "symbol": "circle", "size": 7, "fill": "#FFFFFFCC", "stroke": { "color": "#16697A", "width": 1 } },
      "trendlines": [{ "type": "linear", "stroke": { "color": "#D9A21B", "width": 1.25, "dash": "dash" } }],
      "errorBars": { "valueType": "standard-error", "direction": "y", "type": "both" }
    }]
  }
}
```

Use series defaults when one series needs a different label policy, and use
sparse point overrides only for evidence that needs an exception. Point
indices are zero-based, strictly increasing and must address an existing
non-missing point:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "categories": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
    "series": [{
      "id": "conversion",
      "name": "Conversion",
      "values": [0.18, 0.22, 0.27, 0.31],
      "dataLabels": {
        "showValue": true,
        "numberFormat": "0.0%",
        "textStyle": { "fontSize": 8, "color": "#334155" },
        "points": [
          { "index": 0, "showValue": false },
          { "index": 3, "position": "top", "textStyle": { "bold": true, "color": "#D9A21B" } }
        ]
      }
    }]
  }
}
```

Do not use point labels as a substitute for a readable scale. Custom label
text, manual label layout, label shapes/effects, leader-line graphs and
source-linked number formats remain source-owned and fail closed.

Use `pointStyles` when one real datum needs visual emphasis without rebuilding
the chart as shapes. Keep the list sparse and sorted; a missing observation
cannot be styled. `explosion` is native only on pie and doughnut:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "categories": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
    "series": [{

options, 3D state, effects, extensions and irregular point graphs stay
source-owned rather than being approximated.

rebuilding the visual with shapes:

```

For a circular chart, rotate the first slice only when it improves the reading
path or aligns a declared slice with a label or adjacent explanation. Size a
doughnut hole to reserve a meaningful center annotation; do not rotate slices
or enlarge the hole merely to make the chart look different:

```json
{
  "chartType": "doughnut",
  "style": {
    "legend": "right",
    "startAngle": 135,
    "holeSize": 68,
    "dataLabels": { "showPercent": true, "position": "center" }
  }
}
```

`startAngle` applies only to `pie` and `doughnut`; `holeSize` applies only to
`doughnut`. Imported editable circular charts expose `setChartPlot`. If that
capability is absent, retain the native plot instead of replacing it with
shapes or an image.

When the title needs an emphasized result, keep the title native and use the
same bounded paragraph/run vocabulary as ordinary text:

```json
{
  "title": {
    "paragraphs": [{
      "runs": [
        { "text": "Measured profile: " },
        {
          "text": "−42% incidents",
          "style": {
            "bold": true,
            "color": "#A83232",
            "fontFamilyEastAsia": "Noto Serif CJK SC"
          }
        }
      ]
    }]
  },
  "style": {
    "titleTextStyle": {
      "fontSize": 14,
      "fontFamily": "Aptos",
      "fontFamilyEastAsia": "Noto Sans CJK SC",
      "color": "#16324F"
    }
  }
}
```

`titleTextStyle` is a default for properties omitted by a structured run;
explicit run typography wins. Formula-backed titles, title hyperlinks,
WordArt, effects, and unknown title containers remain source-owned.

`smooth` preserves an explicit true or false native value. `varyColors: true`
authors one direct native color-variation flag; false is canonical omission.
Both line-behavior fields are line-chart-only. Structured chart titles compile
to bounded native DrawingML paragraphs and runs on ordinary and combo charts.
A projected imported chart may issue `setChartTitle` for that title content and
`setChartTextStyle` for uniform title defaults, legend, data labels, axis titles
and tick labels. Each capability authorizes only its declared field. Theme
transforms and other effect-bearing chart text remain source-owned and fail
closed instead of being flattened.

Chart paint uses the same typed fill union as shapes and table cells. This
keeps a gradient semantic rather than rebuilding it from overlaid rectangles:

```json
{
  "style": {
    "chartAreaFill": { "type": "none" },
    "plotAreaFill": {
      "type": "gradient",
      "kind": "radial",
      "stops": [
        { "offset": 0, "color": "#F8FAFC", "opacity": 0.96 },
        { "offset": 1, "color": "#DCE7F2", "opacity": 0.72 }
      ]
    }
  },
  "data": {
    "categories": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
    "series": [{
      "id": "revenue",
      "name": "Revenue",
      "values": [18, 24, 31, 39],
      "fill": {
        "type": "gradient",
        "kind": "linear",
        "angle": 90,
        "stops": [
          { "offset": 0, "color": "#0EA5A8" },
          { "offset": 1, "color": "#0B3A5B", "opacity": 0.82 }
        ]
      }
    }]
  }
}
```

For a simple solid series, `"color": "#0A84FF80"` is a compact authored
alias for the equivalent solid `fill` with alpha. Reimport canonicalizes it to
the structured fill form so the opacity remains explicit and subsequent edits
do not oscillate between two spellings. Use `fill` directly when the series
needs none/gradient paint or a separately named opacity.

The bounded profile accepts two through sixteen ordered direct-RGB stops,
linear angles, and centered radial gradients. Theme transforms, pattern/image
paint, path variants, and irregular native gradient graphs remain
source-preserved. An imported chart must issue `setChartFill`; neither
`setChartData` nor `setChartTextStyle` authorizes paint changes.

The scalar marker spelling and `showDataLabels` / `dataLabelPosition` remain
valid for older PPJ. Do not combine either legacy spelling with its structured
form. On an imported source-bound chart, a `setChartData` capability owns only
series names and values; it cannot be used to smuggle axis, marker, label,
trendline, error-bar or paint changes.

}

Keep files beside the program or inside its\nmanaged asset workspace. Do not place remote URLs, network instructions, or\nlarge base64 payloads in PPJ.\n\nPrefer sources in this order:\n\n1. user-provided, brand, template, or official assets;\n2. evidence images tied to the claim;\n3. rights-compatible editorial or contextual imagery;\n4. generated imagery when the host provides it and its status is recorded;\n5. native vectors or no image when no suitable asset exists.\n\nDo not present a generated or decorative image as documentary evidence. PPJ source-free authoring supports MP4 video and\nMP3, M4A, or WAV audio. Every media element requires an explicit image\n`posterAsset`; the poster is the editable native picture surface seen before\nplayback and in static rendering.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"field-observation\",\n  \"type\": \"media\",\n  \"name\": \"Field observation video\",\n  \"role\": \"primary evidence\",\n  \"frame\": { \"x\": 528, \"y\": 96, \"width\": 360, \"height\": 240 },\n  \"accessibility\": {\n    \"decorative\": false,\n    \"description\": \"A short field observation showing the measured condition.\"\n  },\n  \"mediaType\": \"video\",\n  \"asset\": \"field-observation-mp4\",\n  \"posterAsset\": \"field-observation-poster\",\n  \"startAtMs\": 1200,\n  \"endAtMs\": 400,\n  \"loop\": false,\n  \"mute\": true\n}\n```\n\n`startAtMs` and `endAtMs` are bounded leading and trailing trim offsets, not\ntimeline expressions. `loop` and `mute` compile to native playback state.\nOfficeKit owns the media relationships, click action, canonical timing nodes,\nposter relationship, and package part names; PPJ owns only the typed state\nabove. Keep media below 64 MiB per asset and within the deck's aggregate asset\nbudget.\n\nStatic render and structural review prove the poster and package graph, not\nplayback. Record desktop evidence separately when actual playback matters.\nThird-party media timing remains opaque/source-bound: importing it does not\nauthorize rewriting triggers, bookmarks, effects, or an unfamiliar timing\ngraph.\n\n## Imported paired SVG pictures\n\nSome PowerPoint pictures carry two assets: a PNG or JPEG compatibility image\nin `image.asset` and an SVG for modern hosts in `image.svgAsset`. Treat them as\ndifferent roles. Do not replace the fallback merely because the vector artwork\nis the intended edit.\n\nWhen inspection issues `replaceSvg` for `image.svgAsset`:\n\n1. create a new local `image/svg+xml` asset declaration with exact bytes and\n   SHA-256;\n2. point only `svgAsset` at the new declaration;\n3. keep `asset`, the element ID, frame, crop, nativeRef and array position;\n4. build, re-import and render the edited page.\n\nThe compiler replaces only the proven SVG relationship. It does not create or\nremove a fallback pair and does not rasterize the new SVG. An unchanged raster\nfallback is intentional compatibility state, so legacy-host appearance must be\nchecked separately when it matters. A standalone authored SVG remains an\nordinary `image.asset`; do not add `svgAsset` to source-free PPJ.\n\n## Layer stack\n\n`pages[].elements[]` is the true back-to-front z-order. A common image-led page\nmay use:\n\n```text\nbackground image\n→ crop or color field\n→ scrim/mask for contrast\n→ evidence or identity layer\n→ editable title and annotation\n→ foreground action or source\n```\n\nUse an image as the page `background` when it is a true non-selectable slide\nsurface. PPJ compiles it into native `<p:bg>` image paint, not a backmost picture\nshape. Native image backgrounds support `stretch`, `cover`, `contain`, explicit\nsigned crop, direct opacity, and parameter-free `tile`. Use an image element\nwhen it must remain independently selectable, masked, bordered, shadowed,\nanimated, or reordered.\n\nA native solid background also retains direct opacity. Use either an\nalpha-bearing color or an explicit `opacity`; the explicit value wins:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"background\": {\n    \"type\": \"solid\",\n    \"color\": \"#0A84FF\",\n    \"opacity\": 0.45\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe page owns one background paint, not a stack of background paints. To place\na color scrim over a background photograph, keep the photograph as the native\nimage background and put an ordinary translucent shape first in\n`elements[]`, before foreground text.\n\n### Element visibility and edit locks\n\nAll typed elements can use `hidden` and `locked`. Use `hidden: true` to keep a\nstable object in the program while excluding it from the visible slide. Use\n`locked: true` after a background, guide, media poster, or finished composition\nis placed correctly and should resist accidental selection or movement.\n\nThese fields do not change layer order: `elements[]` remains the only\nback-to-front stack. They also do not hide the page or protect the file from a\nuser with edit access. On an imported deck, change a field only when the\nobject's `nativeRef.capabilities` includes the matching `setHidden` or\n`setLocked`; unfamiliar partial lock combinations remain source-owned.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"background\": {\n    \"type\": \"image\",\n    \"asset\": \"wetland-aerial\",\n    \"fit\": \"cover\",\n    \"opacity\": 0.78\n  }\n}\n```\n\n`cover` and `contain` lower deterministically from the declared asset dimensions\nand slide frame. An explicit `crop` overrides that calculation. `tile` emits\nonly the portable default DrawingML tile profile; arbitrary tile scale, offset,\nalignment, mirroring, external links, and extra image effects fail closed. An\nimported native background can change only when the page `nativeRef` issues\n`setBackground` for that exact source revision.\n\nA page background may also use a native linear or centered radial gradient.\nChoose it as a surface hierarchy or directional-light device, not as substitute\nimagery. Keep the stop count small, maintain text contrast across the entire\nfield, and use a foreground image element when a photographic subject must be\ncropped or animated independently.\n\nUse an image element when it must remain independently selectable, cropped,\nanimated, or reordered. Preset masks, direct opacity, bounded RGB borders, and\none bounded outer shadow belong to that image element; overlays are ordinary\nshapes placed after the image and before text. On imported files, change only\nthe effect values and mask adjustments returned by inspection. Unfamiliar\neffect graphs and custom mask topology stay source-bound instead of being\nflattened.\n\nKeep the subject, intended focal point, and important edges inside the crop.\nUse `cover` for image-led regions, `contain` for diagrams or logos that must not\ncrop, `tile` only for a genuinely repeatable texture, and explicit crop values\nwhen reproducibility matters. Re-render after font, crop, mask, or z-order\nchanges.\n\nShape and text-container fills can use the same bounded native image-paint\nprofile. This is useful when a photograph or texture must be clipped by editable\nshape geometry:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"type\": \"shape\",\n  \"id\": \"material-window\",\n  \"frame\": { \"x\": 72, \"y\": 110, \"width\": 360, \"height\": 250 },\n  \"geometry\": { \"kind\": \"preset\", \"preset\": \"arc\" },\n  \"style\": {\n    \"fill\": {\n      \"type\": \"image\",\n      \"asset\": \"material-photo\",\n      \"fit\": \"cover\",\n      \"opacity\": 0.9\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThis creates a real `a:blipFill` on the shape. It is not a rasterized silhouette.\nImported canonical image fills project back into PPJ and may be changed only\nwhen `nativeRef.capabilities` issues `setFill`.\n\n## Image masks\n\nA preset image mask is native editable geometry, not a rasterized cutout. It\nuses the same finite profile table as a shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"type\": \"image\",\n  \"id\": \"portrait\",\n  \"frame\": { \"x\": 612, \"y\": 92, \"width\": 252, \"height\": 336 },\n  \"asset\": \"portrait-photo\",\n  \"fit\": \"cover\",\n  \"mask\": {\n    \"kind\": \"preset\",\n    \"preset\": \"round2SameRect\",\n    \"adjustments\": [18000, 6000]\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe adjustment array is complete or omitted for native defaults. Its order and\ndefaults come from the [generated PPJ preset table](ppj.md#preset-geometry-adjustments).\nAn imported picture can change only these values when `nativeRef.capabilities`\nissues `setImageMask`; the preset identity, crop, asset, frame, and native\ntopology remain fixed.\n\nUse a custom mask only when the silhouette carries a real editorial or brand\nrole that no preset geometry expresses. It uses the same finite literal-path\nvocabulary as a custom shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"type\": \"image\",\n  \"id\": \"field-photo\",\n  \"frame\": { \"x\": 552, \"y\": 72, \"width\": 360, \"height\": 396 },\n  \"asset\": \"field-photo\",\n  \"fit\": \"cover\",\n  \"mask\": {\n    \"kind\": \"custom\",\n    \"viewBox\": { \"x\": 0, \"y\": 0, \"width\": 160, \"height\": 160 },\n    \"paths\": [{\n      \"fill\": true,\n      \"stroke\": false,\n      \"commands\": [\n        { \"op\": \"moveTo\", \"x\": 20, \"y\": 0 },\n        { \"op\": \"lineTo\", \"x\": 160, \"y\": 0 },\n        { \"op\": \"lineTo\", \"x\": 140, \"y\": 160 },\n        { \"op\": \"lineTo\", \"x\": 0, \"y\": 120 },\n        { \"op\": \"close\" }\n      ]\n    }]\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe compiler writes a native picture `<a:custGeom>`; it does not rasterize the\nmask. Keep the path count and command count small, and do not invent irregular\nblobs merely to decorate empty space. Canonical imported literal masks can be\ninspected and projected into PPJ, but their path topology remains source-owned:\nwithout a separately issued mutation capability, changing those paths fails\nbefore output. Guide formulas, handles, connection sites, text rectangles and\nother richer custom-geometry graphs remain opaque-preserved.\n\n## Protect content\n\nText contrast must survive the actual image, not an imagined average color.\nScrims should be only strong enough to establish hierarchy. Decorative fields\nmay overlap each other, but may not hide text, sources, chart evidence, product\ndetails, or the image subject.\n\nAvoid repeated stock photographs, identical hero crops, gratuitous shadows,\nfull-page texture that reduces legibility, and photo mosaics without a narrative\nrelationship. A page can be image-free when data, geometry, or typography is\nthe stronger carrier.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

It prevents the agent\nfrom spending its first decisions on shapes instead of communication. It does\nnot prescribe a palette, font, template, or layout.\n\n## Before composing\n\nWrite one compact contract before adding elements. Record it in the existing\nPPJ `intent`, `design.grammar`, and page-planning fields; do not invent a new\nschema just for this checklist.\n\n```text\nAudience task: what must this audience know, believe, decide, or do?\nOne conclusion: what is the sentence the page must leave behind?\nPrimary carrier: what carries the conclusion—chart, image, diagram, text,\n  table, native vector, or a deliberate mix?\nReading order: what should be seen first, second, and third?\nProtected evidence: which bars, lines, labels, numbers, axes, sources,\n  image subjects, or relationships may not be hidden or cropped?\nCanvas occupancy: which regions are intentionally active, quiet, or reserved?\nLayer order: what is background, scrim, evidence, annotation, and foreground?\nForbidden shortcut: which filler pattern would make this page generic?\n```\n\nThe contract should fit in a few lines. If the conclusion or carrier is still\nunclear, resolve that uncertainty before composing. If the page intentionally\nuses sparse composition, say why the quiet area creates focus, separation, or\nrhythm.\n\n## Choose the carrier by relationship\n\n- Use a chart when magnitude, change, distribution, or uncertainty is the\n  claim. Give axes, units, labels, and annotations enough room to remain true.\n- Use a diagram when sequence, hierarchy, causality, flow, or spatial\n  relationship is itself the evidence. Every connector and node needs a role.\n- Use an image or SVG when a real subject, place, product, identity, or\n  atmosphere carries meaning. Keep the focal subject inside the crop and keep\n  attribution or evidence boundaries visible.\n- Use typography when the conclusion is the evidence. Establish hierarchy by\n  scale, measure, line, and rhythm rather than by a wall of containers.\n- Use a deliberate mix only when the objects explain one another. A chart,\n  image, and text block that merely coexist is not an information relationship.\n\n## Compose in attention order\n\n1. Place the primary carrier and give it enough area to be read at final size.\n2. Place the conclusion and the smallest supporting labels needed to interpret\n   that carrier.\n3. Add decision, comparison, or uncertainty annotations only where they\n   change the reading.\n4. Add source, assumption, and accessibility text without hiding evidence.\n5. Add a background, scrim, mask, line, or small motif only when its layer\n   role is explicit. Do not use decoration to repair an empty page.\n\nUse `pages[].elements[]` as a true back-to-front stack. A foreground object\nmust never cover a bar, line, marker, error bar, number, axis, source, image\nsubject, or connector that carries the page's claim. For combo charts, reserve\nseparate label clearances instead of forcing a line through a data label or\nmaking a bar transparent merely to hide a layering mistake.\n\nNative chart defaults are not a label plan. For a chart with more than a few\ncategories, explicitly configure data labels to show only the values the\nreader needs; set category, series, and percentage labels off unless each is\ndeliberately useful. A series name belongs in a legend or one heading, never\nrepeated beside every data point. If only two endpoints are known, use endpoint\nmarks or a clearly two-point comparison; do not draw a continuous line that\nsuggests unobserved intermediate values. A `null` gap is not enough without a\nrender check because hosts can bridge sparse points. A syntactically valid chart\nwhose labels collide, repeat, or imply unsupported data is a failed page.\n\n**Sparse-observation route.** Count the observed points before choosing a\nshared-axis chart. Keep the\ncomparison outside the unrelated series' plot and name the observation window\nin its heading. A native sparse line is allowed only when the user explicitly\nrequests it, the x positions are truly observed, and a final-size render shows\nno bridge, collision, or false continuity. Never hide a sparse line with a\ntransparent stroke and leave a line legend behind.\n\n## Four executable quality contracts\n\nUse these contracts while composing and during the single render-correction\npass. They are implementation rules, not suggestions for a visual style.\n\n**Chart labels.** Before building a chart, state the label budget: which marks\nneed a value, category, series name, or percentage. Set all four visibility\nflags explicitly (`showValue`, `showCategory`, `showSeries`, `showPercent`).\nFor six or more categories, default to no per-mark labels; add only short,\nnon-repeating labels or sparse endpoint labels that carry the claim. Put a\nseries name in one legend or heading. If a label collides at final size,\nremove, shorten, or relocate the label; never shrink the whole page to save it.\n\n**Missing data.** Represent an unobserved value with `null` and disclose the\ngap in the chart or source note. Never coerce it to zero, interpolate it, or\nconnect two observed endpoints through missing categories. Treat occlusion, clipping, unreadable text, false evidence, and\nchanged non-target content as blocking issues.\n\n## What this contract does not do\n\nIt does not force dark or light themes, a particular number of images, a\nspecific geometry vocabulary, or a fixed page template. User templates,\nbrand systems, imported design, and the deck's own grammar remain authoritative.\nThe contract only makes the reasoning that precedes composition explicit and\nreviewable.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Every recommendation must point to evidence or an explicit assumption.\nCounter-evidence belongs near the claim it limits.\n\n## Narrative\n\nFrame the decision, establish criteria, show the evidence and alternatives,\nsurface uncertainty, recommend a path, then make the next decision explicit.\nPut decisive evidence before the recommendation. OfficeKit keeps the\nlogical point count and writes a native chart gap; it does not coerce the value\nto zero or invent an estimate. They cannot call themselves recursively. Expanded\nIDs are deterministic. A component is reuse, not a hidden script.\n\n## Imported PPTX and nativeRef\n\nImport copies the source package into a content-addressed local asset and binds\nits SHA-256. Every visible object becomes a typed element or `opaque` with a\n`nativeRef`. A nativeRef lists only capability-issued fields. Edit those\nfields and keep its expected revision/hash; unsupported topology stays opaque.\nNo-op build returns the source bytes exactly. A stale, ambiguous or undeclared\nmutation fails instead of rebuilding or flattening the source.\n\n### Imported presentation canvas\n\nAn imported `design.canvas` is editable only when its own `nativeRef` issues\n`setCanvas` for `canvas.width` and `canvas.height`. Values stay in points.\nKeep the nativeRef unchanged, edit one or both dimensions, then build and\nre-import. The compiler changes only the native presentation canvas: it never\nscales, reflows, crops or moves slide, layout, master or element coordinates.\nBecause every page is composed against that canvas, render and review every\npage for exposed margins, clipping and changed balance after the edit.\n\n### Imported raster/SVG fallback pairs\n\nPowerPoint may store one visible picture as a raster compatibility fallback\nplus an SVG used by modern hosts. PPJ projects these as two local assets:\n\n- `image.asset` is the raster fallback;\n- `image.svgAsset` is the true SVG member.\n\nChange `svgAsset` only when that image's `nativeRef` issues `replaceSvg` for\n`image.svgAsset`. Declare the replacement as a new content-addressed local\n`image/svg+xml` asset, keep `asset`, the image ID and nativeRef unchanged,\nthen build and re-import. PPJ cannot add or remove the pair and does not invent\na raster fallback. Review the modern SVG render; when an older host matters,\nrecord separately that its unchanged raster fallback may still show the prior\nartwork.\n\n### Closed imported leaf vocabulary\n\nThe max 9999 |\n| `fill` | no | `fill` | none |\n| `stroke` | no | `stroke` | none |\n| `explosion` | no | `integer` | min 0; max 400 |\n\n\n--- CHARTS REF 1 ---\n# Charts and tables\n\nChoose the visual from the relationship the audience must understand.\n\n| Relationship | Prefer |\n| --- | --- |\n| trend or change over ordered time | line, area, or ordered columns |\n| changing composition and total magnitude over ordered time | streamgraph |\n| magnitude across categories | bars or columns with a common baseline |\n| small exact counts where one repeated glyph has a declared unit | pictographic bar or column |\n| distribution or correlation | scatter, bubble, or distribution view |\n| intensity across two categorical dimensions | heatmap |\n| open/high/low/close movement over ordered periods | candlestick |\n| hierarchical part-to-whole allocation | treemap |\n| hierarchical part-to-whole path across concentric levels | sunburst |\n| conserved magnitude moving through a directed process | sankey |\n| multivariate profile across a small shared scale | standard radar |\n| contribution to change | waterfall |\n| precise lookup or rule comparison | table |\n| mixed measures sharing a truthful category axis | deliberate combo chart |\n\nAvoid pies with many categories, decorative 3D, dual axes without a necessary\nand clearly labelled relationship, truncated scales that exaggerate change,\nand a chart that merely repeats one large number.\n\n## Evidence integrity\n\n- Preserve source values, units, time windows, denominators, and uncertainty.\n- Use direct labels where they reduce legend lookup.\n- Keep common scales for comparisons that claim comparability.\n- Show missing values and estimates honestly.\n- Put the exact source and as-of date on the page or in a visible source area.\n\nTreat native data-label defaults as unsafe. Configure `showValue`,\n`showCategory`, `showSeries`, and `showPercent` explicitly at the smallest\nscope that communicates the claim. Keep a series name in one legend or\nheading, not repeated beside every mark. For endpoint-only evidence, use two\nendpoint marks or a visibly two-point comparison; never let a renderer bridge\nmissing categories into an invented continuous trend. Render the chart at\nfinal size and remove any label collision before delivery, even when structural\nreview passes.\n\nWhen a series contains only two observations, prefer a separate endpoint\ncomparison instead of adding a sparse line to a multi-series time axis. The\ncomparison may be two large values, a dumbbell without intermediate ticks, or a\ntwo-category bar chart (`baseline`, `current`). State the exact observation\nwindow in the heading and keep the unrelated chart's scale independent. A\nshared-axis sparse line requires an explicit user request and a render proving\nthat the host preserves a gap; a valid PPJ shape is not evidence of a truthful\ntrend.\n\nUse JSON `null` for a genuinely missing Y observation. OfficeKit keeps the\nlogical point count and writes a native chart gap; it does not coerce the value\nto zero or invent an estimate. This works for the bounded authored chart\nfamilies, including numeric scatter/bubble Y values. Numeric `xValues` and\n`bubbleSizes` remain complete arrays. In a source-bound chart, edit measured\nvalues around an existing gap, but do not add or remove gaps: missing-point\ntopology remains tied to the exact source cache.\n\nLines, markers, labels, confidence intervals, error bars, and decision\nthresholds are protected foreground evidence. Bars, areas, fills, masks, and\nannotations may not hide them. For truthful combo charts, first keep the real\nshared plot, render the line above pale or transparent bars, reserve clearance\naround markers, and re-anchor only colliding labels. Split into aligned panels\nonly when the units are incompatible or the truthful shared plot remains\nillegible after those repairs.\n\nDo not force separation merely to make a checker quiet. Do not change scale,\ndata, or category position to manufacture whitespace.\n\n## PPJ structure\n\nChart elements keep a stable `id`, explicit `frame`, typed `chartType`, data,\nand style. Tables declare column widths and typed rows; they are not collections\nof manually aligned text boxes. Use chart/table styles to define semantic\nroles, then override only when a specific datum needs emphasis.\n\nChart and table frames may use `rotation`, `flipH`, and `flipV`. These are real\nnative graphic-frame transforms and survive PPJ build, import, and a\ncapability-issued source edit. Prefer ordinary zero-degree evidence layouts;\nrotate a chart or table only when the orientation itself communicates a real\nspatial relationship, never to decorate a page.\n\nThe authored chart compiler owns these native visual controls:\n\n- bar, column, line, area, pie, doughnut, scatter, bubble, standard radar,\n  bounded semantic waterfall, bounded vector heatmap, bounded vector\n  candlestick, bounded vector streamgraph, bounded vector pictographic bars and\n  columns, bounded vector treemap, bounded vector sunburst, bounded vector\n  sankey, bounded column-line-area category combo plots, and bounded editable\n  scatter/bubble plus line/area/column numeric overlays;\n- legend visibility and top, bottom, left, or right placement;\n- ordinary, stacked, and percent-stacked grouping where the chart family\n  supports it;\n- pie/doughnut first-slice orientation from 0 through 360 degrees and\n  doughnut center-hole size from 10 through 90 percent;\n- bubble scale from 0 through 300 percent and native size interpretation by\n  bubble area or width;\n- bar direction, gap width, category/value-axis visibility, major gridlines,\n  data-label visibility and bounded label position;\n- presence-aware axis reversal plus direct RGB/no-fill axis and major-grid\n  lines with bounded width, dash, opacity, cap, and join;\n- chart-area, plot-area, and series none, solid, or bounded direct-RGB gradient\n  fills, including solid and per-stop opacity;\n- editable series line width, dash, opacity, cap, join, and bounded markers;\n- category/value-axis titles, number formats, label interval, tick-label\n  typeface, size, bold, italic and direct RGB/alpha, value bounds and major\n  unit; bounded combo charts may declare the matching secondary pair;\n- chart-title Latin/East Asian typeface, size, bold, italic and direct\n  RGB/alpha plus canonical line-chart smoothing and direct color variation;\n- structured data labels for value, category, series, percentage, native\n  position, direct number format and bounded typography at plot, series and\n  sparse point scope;\n- sparse point fill, outline and pie/doughnut explosion for measured exceptions;\n- direct marker symbol, size, RGB/alpha fill and bounded stroke;\n- exponential, linear, logarithmic, moving-average, polynomial and power\n  trendlines on bar, column and line series;\n- fixed-value, percentage, standard-deviation and standard-error error bars on\n  bar, column and line series.\n\nUse the analytical fields as chart semantics, not as decorative paint. A page can be image-free when data, geometry, or typography is\\nthe stronger carrier.\\n--- VISUAL ATTENTION ---\\n# Visual attention contract\\n\\nUse this reference when creating a page from a brief, selecting a visual\\ndirection, or materially redesigning an imported page. It prevents the agent\\nfrom spending its first decisions on shapes instead of communication. It does\\nnot prescribe a palette, font, template, or layout.\\n\\n## Before composing\\n\\nWrite one compact contract before adding elements. Record it in the existing\\nPPJ `intent`, `design.grammar`, and page-planning fields; do not invent a new\\nschema just for this checklist.\\n\\n```text\\nAudience task: what must this audience know, believe, decide, or do?\\nOne conclusion: what is the sentence the page must leave behind?\\nPrimary carrier: what carries the conclusion—chart, image, diagram, text,\\n  table, native vector, or a deliberate mix?\\nReading order: what should be seen first, second, and third?\\nProtected evidence: which bars, lines, labels, numbers, axes, sources,\\n  image subjects, or relationships may not be hidden or cropped?\\nCanvas occupancy: which regions are intentionally active, quiet, or reserved?\\nLayer order: what is background, scrim, evidence, annotation, and foreground?\\nForbidden shortcut: which filler pattern would make this page generic?\\n```\\n\\nThe contract should fit in a few lines. If the conclusion or carrier is still\\nunclear, resolve that uncertainty before composing. If the page intentionally\\nuses sparse composition, say why the quiet area creates focus, separation, or\\nrhythm.\\n\\n## Choose the carrier by relationship\\n\\n- Use a chart when magnitude, change, distribution, or uncertainty is the\\n  claim. Give axes, units, labels, and annotations enough room to remain true.\\n- Use a diagram when sequence, hierarchy, causality, flow, or spatial\\n  relationship is itself the evidence. Every connector and node needs a role.\\n- Use an image or SVG when a real subject, place, product, identity, or\\n  atmosphere carries meaning. Keep the focal subject inside the crop and keep\\n  attribution or evidence boundaries visible.\\n- Use typography when the conclusion is the evidence. Establish hierarchy by\\n  scale, measure, line, and rhythm rather than by a wall of containers.\\n- Use a deliberate mix only when the objects explain one another. A chart,\\n  image, and text block that merely coexist is not an information relationship.\\n\\n## Compose in attention order\\n\\n1. Place the primary carrier and give it enough area to be read at final size.\\n2. Place the conclusion and the smallest supporting labels needed to interpret\\n   that carrier.\\n3. Add decision, comparison, or uncertainty annotations only where they\\n   change the reading.\\n4. Add source, assumption, and accessibility text without hiding evidence.\\n5. Add a background, scrim, mask, line, or small motif only when its layer\\n   role is explicit. Do not use decoration to repair an empty page.\\n\\nUse `pages[].elements[]` as a true back-to-front stack. A foreground object\\nmust never cover a bar, line, marker, error bar, number, axis, source, image\\nsubject, or connector that carries the page's claim. For combo charts, reserve\\nseparate label clearances instead of forcing a line through a data label or\\nmaking a bar transparent merely to hide a layering mistake.\\n\\nNative chart defaults are not a label plan. For a chart with more than a few\\ncategories, explicitly configure data labels to show only the values the\\nreader needs; set category, series, and percentage labels off unless each is\\ndeliberately useful. A series name belongs in a legend or one heading, never\\nrepeated beside every data point. If only two endpoints are known, use endpoint\\nmarks or a clearly two-point comparison; do not draw a continuous line that\\nsuggests unobserved intermediate values. A `null` gap is not enough without a\\nrender check because hosts can bridge sparse points. A syntactically valid chart\\nwhose labels collide, repeat, or imply unsupported data is a failed page.\\n\\n**Sparse-observation route.** Count the observed points before choosing a\\nshared-axis chart. If a series has only two observed points, or more than half\\nof its category values are missing, do not put it on a time/category line or\\ncombo chart by default. Route it to an independent endpoint comparison:\\ntwo labelled metrics, a dumbbell with no intermediate ticks, or two aligned\\nbars whose categories are explicitly `baseline` and `current`. Keep the\\ncomparison outside the unrelated series' plot and name the observation window\\nin its heading. A native sparse line is allowed only when the user explicitly\\nrequests it, the x positions are truly observed, and a final-size render shows\\nno bridge, collision, or false continuity. Never hide a sparse line with a\\ntransparent stroke and leave a line legend behind.\\n\\n## Four executable quality contracts\\n\\nUse these contracts while composing and during the single render-correction\\npass. They are implementation rules, not suggestions for a visual style.\\n\\n**Chart labels.** Before building a chart, state the label budget: which marks\\nneed a value, category, series name, or percentage. Set all four visibility\\nflags explicitly (`showValue`, `showCategory`, `showSeries`, `showPercent`).\\nFor six or more categories, default to no per-mark labels; add only short,\\nnon-repeating labels or sparse endpoint labels that carry the claim. Put a\\nseries name in one legend or heading. If a label collides at final size,\\nremove, shorten, or relocate the label; never shrink the whole page to save it.\\n\\n**Missing data.** Represent an unobserved value with `null` and disclose the\\ngap in the chart or source note. Never coerce it to zero, interpolate it, or\\nconnect two observed endpoints through missing categories. If the renderer\\nbridges `null`, replace the line with endpoint marks, a two-point comparison,\\nor separate observed segments. A visual trend is a data claim, so the chosen\\nmark must match the observation topology.\\n\\n**Layer and occlusion.** Write a short stack before adding overlays:\\n`background → scrim → carrier → evidence marks → labels/annotations →\\nforeground/source`. For each overlay, name the evidence it is allowed to\\ntouch. No object may cover a bar, line, marker, error bar, axis, data label,\\nsource, image subject, or connector. Preserve truthful shared plots; use\\nopacity, clearance, or a separate annotation only when it keeps the measured\\nrelationship visible. Do not separate objects, move a scale, or use\\ntransparency merely to silence a checker.\\n\\n**Render correction.** The minimum loop is `check → build → render at final\\nsize → inspect high-risk regions → repair the smallest source field → render\\nagain`. A structural pass is not a visual pass. Stop and report\\n`visualReview: unavailable` when the page cannot be inspected; do not deliver\\nan unreviewed candidate. Treat any evidence occlusion, label collision,\\nclipping, false trend, unreadable text, or accidental empty region as a\\nblocking issue. Keep the correction local and record what changed; do not\\nrewrite the deck to hide a failed page.\\n\\n## 1→10 edits\\n\\nFor an existing page, inspect before editing:\\n\\n- current carrier and conclusion;\\n- current reading order and z-order;\\n- evidence that must remain stable;\\n- intentional quiet areas and background layers;\\n- whether the request is local or a global redesign.\\n\\nFor a local edit, keep every untouched element, source, crop, and layer in\\nplace. Do not add a new accent, card, image, or global rewrite simply because\\nthe edited object leaves more space. For a redesign, write a replacement\\ncontract and review all affected pages for rhythm and design drift.\\n\\n## Review questions\\n\\nAnswer these from the rendered page, not from PPJ alone:\\n\\n- Can a reader state the page conclusion without guessing?\\n- Is the primary carrier visibly dominant and large enough?\\n- Does the reading order follow scale, position, and contrast?\\n- Is every protected evidence object visible and legible?\\n- Does each quiet region have a declared purpose?\\n- Is any object present only to fill space or imitate a template?\\n- Do background images, masks, scrims, and overlays preserve contrast?\\n- Did a local edit change anything outside its requested surface?\\n\\nWarnings are appropriate for weak hierarchy, repeated rhythm, or low\\noccupancy. Treat occlusion, clipping, unreadable text, false evidence, and\\nchanged non-target content as blocking issues.\\n\\n## What this contract does not do\\n\\nIt does not force dark or light themes, a particular number of images, a\\nspecific geometry vocabulary, or a fixed page template. User templates,\\nbrand systems, imported design, and the deck's own grammar remain authoritative.\\nThe contract only makes the reasoning that precedes composition explicit and\\nreviewable.\\n--- ANALYSIS DECISION ---\\n# Scenario: analysis and decision\\n\\n## Audience task\\n\\nHelp an informed audience compare evidence, understand tradeoffs, and make a\\nspecific decision. The deck should reduce uncertainty rather than manufacture\\nconfidence.\\n\\nLock the decision, criteria, time horizon, baseline, and uncertainty before\\ndrawing. Every recommendation must point to evidence or an explicit assumption.\\nCounter-evidence belongs near the claim it limits.\\n\\n## Narrative\\n\\nFrame the decision, establish criteria, show the evidence and alternatives,\\nsurface uncertainty, recommend a path, then make the next decision explicit.\\nPut decisive evidence before the recommendation. Use an appendix for audit\\ndetail, not for facts required to understand the choice.\\n\\nUseful page jobs include decision frame, baseline, driver analysis, option\\ncomparison, sensitivity or scenario range, recommendation, conditions, and\\nnext action. Do not force all of them into one fixed sequence.\\n\\n## Density and rhythm\\n\\nAlternate compact decision frames with denser evidence pages. Preserve common\\nscales across comparable charts. Give exceptions and uncertainty enough space\\nto be read. A live deck may stage a complex driver chain; a reader deck must\\nremain self-contained without the animation.\\n\\n## Relationship-to-carrier choices\\n\\n- annotated trend, variance, waterfall, or distribution chart;\\n- option comparison on shared criteria and a common visual scale;\\n- driver tree, causal chain, or sensitivity map;\\n- evidence table with one decision-relevant row or threshold highlighted;\\n- recommendation page with conditions, trigger, owner, and next action;\\n- scenario range rather than a single false-precision forecast.\\n\\nCharts should encode a relationship, not decorate a number. Tables work when\\nexact values or criteria matter. Diagrams work when causal structure matters.\\nUse sourced imagery only when the physical context changes the decision; do not\\nuse a generic market image as the evidence carrier.\\n\\n## Visual grammar\\n\\nUse restrained surfaces, straight geometry, explicit axes, thin dividers, and\\none high-contrast decision role. Prefer direct labels, aligned baselines, and\\nconsistent units. Use boxes only when they encode comparable alternatives or\\nbounded states. Connectors must carry direction, dependency, or causality.\\n\\nTypography should separate claim, evidence annotation, and source. Spacing\\nshould make the decision path scannable without turning every observation into\\na card. Motifs may mark thresholds or selected options, but must not become a\\nsecond legend.\\n\\nFor a bar-line or other combo chart, preserve one truthful category or time\\nplot when the comparison depends on it. Keep the line and markers above pale or\\ntransparent bars, reserve clearance around every marker, and re-anchor only the\\nlabels that collide. Split into aligned panels only when sharing a plot would\\nmisrepresent the units or remains illegible after those repairs; never split\\nmerely to silence an overlap warning.\\n\\n## Avoid\\n\\nDashboard walls, ornamental KPI cards, incomparable scales, decorative arrows,\\nequal emphasis on every metric, recommendations before evidence, hidden\\nuncertainty, and confidence language unsupported by the source.\\n\\n## Review questions\\n\\n- Can the audience state the decision, criteria, and uncertainty after a scan?\\n- Does each visual change the decision, or merely decorate a number?\\n- Can every line, marker, value label, axis, interval, and error bar be traced\\n  without another series obscuring it?\\n- Are counter-evidence and assumptions visible before the conclusion?\\n- Is the requested action explicit, bounded, and supported?\\n- If the page feels generic, should the claim/evidence or carrier change before\\n  palette and styling are
